title: Asthma: Prove Variable Airflow Disease, Then Step Treatment to Control and Risk
bottomLine: Asthma is a variable inflammatory airway disease that should be objectively confirmed whenever feasible. Management uses inhaled-corticosteroid-containing therapy, inhaler-technique/adherence review and stepwise adjustment based on symptom control, exacerbation risk and phenotype rather than repeated short-acting bronchodilator rescue alone.
recognize: Variable wheeze, dyspnea, cough/chest tightness and trigger-related symptoms support asthma, especially with night/early-morning or episodic patterns.
Normal spirometry between episodes does not exclude asthma; objective variability may require bronchodilator response, serial measurements or another validated test.
differentiate: COPD, inducible laryngeal obstruction, heart failure, bronchiectasis and anxiety can mimic or coexist with asthma.
Fixed obstruction can occur in longstanding asthma and should not automatically relabel the patient as COPD.
assessment: Assess symptom frequency, nighttime waking, activity limitation, reliever/controller use, exacerbations/systemic steroid courses, ED/hospital history, smoking/vaping, occupational triggers, rhinitis and reflux.
Check inhaler device technique and actual adherence before escalating pharmacotherapy.
workup: Use quality spirometry with bronchodilator testing when possible; use alternative objective variability testing when spirometry is nondiagnostic and suspicion remains.
Phenotype/eosinophil/allergy testing is selective and most useful when severe/refractory disease or biologic therapy is being considered.
management: Use a CTS-consistent inhaled-corticosteroid-containing treatment strategy and step up/down according to control and risk after checking diagnosis, technique and adherence.
Provide an individualized written action plan and address triggers, smoking/vaping, vaccination and comorbid upper-airway disease.
Severe/difficult-to-control asthma warrants specialist assessment rather than indefinite addition of systemic steroids.
medicationSafety: LABA monotherapy is unsafe in asthma; long-acting bronchodilator therapy must be paired with appropriate inhaled corticosteroid treatment.
Repeated oral corticosteroid bursts carry cumulative metabolic, bone, psychiatric and infection harms and should trigger controller optimization/specialist review.
redFlags: Silent chest or markedly reduced air movement
Poor response to repeated bronchodilator therapy
counselling: Teach controller versus reliever roles using the patient's actual device and action plan.
Explain that feeling better after bronchodilator does not replace anti-inflammatory control.
followUp: Reassess after treatment changes for symptoms, exacerbations, inhaler technique, adherence and lung function when useful.
Step down only after sustained control and with an action/follow-up plan.
examTrap: Escalating asthma medication without confirming diagnosis or fixing inhaler technique—or treating persistent asthma with rescue bronchodilator alone.
oneLinePearl: Asthma care is objective diagnosis plus anti-inflammatory control, not rescue inhalers alone.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society current Asthma guideline (2021)

title: COPD: Confirm Persistent Obstruction, Then Treat Symptoms and Exacerbation Risk
bottomLine: COPD requires compatible exposure/symptoms plus persistent post-bronchodilator airflow obstruction. Management is not based on FEV1 alone: combine dyspnea, exacerbation history, inhaler technique/adherence, smoking exposure and comorbidities to choose bronchodilator and selected inhaled-corticosteroid therapy.
recognize: Progressive exertional dyspnea, chronic cough/sputum and recurrent lower-respiratory exacerbations in a patient with smoking or other inhalational exposure support suspicion.
Spirometry is required to confirm persistent airflow obstruction; symptoms alone are not enough.
differentiate: Asthma can coexist and changes inhaled-corticosteroid safety; bronchiectasis, HF, ILD and deconditioning can mimic or add to symptoms.
An acute COPD exacerbation is a clinical change in dyspnea/cough/sputum and should not be diagnosed from chest x-ray or sputum colour alone.
assessment: Assess symptoms/function, exacerbations/hospitalizations, inhaler technique/adherence, smoking/vaping, occupational exposure, BMI/nutrition, vaccination, oxygenation and cardiovascular disease.
Consider alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency testing according to current CTS targeted-testing guidance when phenotype/risk supports it.
workup: Use post-bronchodilator spirometry to confirm diagnosis and additional PFT/imaging when symptoms are disproportionate or another disease is suspected.
During exacerbation, use chest imaging/labs selectively to evaluate pneumonia, HF, PE or respiratory failure.
management: Smoking cessation is the highest-value disease-modifying intervention for current smokers; also use vaccination, exercise/pulmonary rehabilitation and inhaler education.
Use long-acting bronchodilators according to symptom and exacerbation burden; add inhaled corticosteroid selectively when exacerbation/eosinophilic/asthma features support benefit.
Exacerbation with respiratory failure, severe hypoxemia, inability to manage at home or major comorbidity requires hospital-level care.
medicationSafety: Inhaled corticosteroids increase pneumonia/thrush risk and should not be added automatically to every COPD regimen.
Long-term oxygen and long-term NIV have specific stable-state indications and should not be prescribed from one acute exacerbation reading.
counselling: Teach inhaler technique, exacerbation action planning and smoking/vaping cessation support.
Explain why increasing inhalers is not a substitute for pulmonary rehabilitation and exposure control.
followUp: Track symptoms, exacerbations, device technique/adherence and spirometry when it will change care.
Reassess oxygen need after recovery from an acute exacerbation.
examTrap: Diagnosing COPD without spirometry—or adding inhaled corticosteroid automatically because FEV1 is low despite no exacerbation/asthma indication.
oneLinePearl: COPD is confirmed by spirometry but treated by the whole patient: symptoms, exacerbations, exposures and comorbidity.
sourceBasis: Canadian Thoracic Society 2023 COPD pharmacotherapy guideline
Canadian Thoracic Society 2025 Alpha-1 Antitrypsin Deficiency guideline

title: Pneumonia: Community vs Health-Care Exposure Changes Risk, but Severity Changes Disposition
bottomLine: Pneumonia requires a compatible clinical syndrome plus objective lower-respiratory evidence when feasible. Separate community-acquired from hospital/health-care-associated pathogen risks, assess severity and host factors, and choose empiric antibiotics from current local guidance rather than automatically broadening therapy because the patient has recent health-care contact.
recognize: Fever, cough, dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachypnea, hypoxemia and focal findings can occur, but older/frail adults may present with confusion or functional decline.
New consolidation on imaging supports pneumonia; normal vitals and normal chest examination substantially reduce probability in many ambulatory patients.
differentiate: Acute bronchitis is usually viral and lacks objective pneumonia evidence.
HF, PE, aspiration pneumonitis and COPD/asthma exacerbation can mimic pneumonia.

Hospital-acquired pneumonia develops after meaningful inpatient exposure and should be evaluated using local resistance/organism risk rather than the obsolete blanket concept that every health-care contact means broad-spectrum therapy.
assessment: Assess oxygenation, respiratory rate, BP, mental status, oral intake, frailty/comorbidity, aspiration risk, recent antibiotics/hospitalization and prior resistant organisms.
Use a validated severity/disposition aid only as support; clinical judgment and social safety still matter.
workup: Use chest radiography when pneumonia is clinically plausible and available; obtain cultures/viral testing according to severity, host risk and whether results will change therapy.
Do not send routine broad microbiology for every mild outpatient CAP.
management: Use current Canadian/local CAP or hospital-acquired pneumonia guidance, local antibiograms and patient allergy/renal/hepatic context.
Treat hypoxemia and sepsis promptly and arrange hospital care for instability, severe frailty, inability to maintain oral therapy or serious comorbidity.
Reassess antibiotic spectrum/duration when microbiology and clinical response clarify the diagnosis.
medicationSafety: Avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum therapy because C. difficile, nephrotoxicity and resistance harms are real.
Renal function, QT risk, drug interactions and allergy history influence antibiotic selection.
counselling: Explain expected recovery and when worsening dyspnea, confusion, persistent fever or inability to hydrate requires urgent reassessment.
followUp: Ensure culture results and duration are closed-loop; repeat imaging only when clinically indicated by age/risk/nonresolution rather than routinely in every recovered patient.
examTrap: Calling bronchitis pneumonia from crackles alone—or choosing maximal broad-spectrum therapy only because the patient had recent health-care contact.
oneLinePearl: Pneumonia treatment follows objective syndrome, severity and organism risk—not anxiety or venue alone.
sourceBasis: Choosing Wisely Canada respiratory antibiotic stewardship
Canadian/local CAP and hospital-acquired pneumonia pathways

title: Pulmonary Embolism: Diagnose by Probability, Treat by Early Risk
bottomLine: Suspected PE is a probability-driven diagnostic problem; confirmed PE is a risk-stratification problem. Use pretest probability to decide D-dimer/imaging, then use hemodynamics, clinical severity and right-heart injury/strain to determine outpatient anticoagulation versus monitored or advanced therapy.
recognize: Acute dyspnea, pleuritic pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis, presyncope/syncope or unexplained hypoxemia can occur.
Pregnancy/estrogen, cancer, surgery, immobilization, prior VTE and thrombophilia raise probability but no single risk factor diagnoses PE.
differentiate: D-dimer is most useful in low/intermediate pretest probability; a positive result is not diagnostic.
High-risk PE is defined by hemodynamic instability/shock context, while intermediate risk incorporates clinical score/right-ventricular injury or strain—not clot size alone.
assessment: Assess hemodynamics, oxygenation, bleeding risk, VTE provoking factors, pregnancy, cancer, renal function and contraindications to anticoagulation/thrombolysis.
Use a validated clinical probability and severity approach rather than gestalt alone when applicable.
workup: Use D-dimer selectively and CTPA/VQ imaging according to probability, renal/pregnancy context and local pathway.
In confirmed PE, assess right-ventricular strain/injury and severity when this changes disposition or escalation.
management: Begin anticoagulation when indicated and choose agent/duration based on hemodynamics, renal function, cancer, pregnancy, bleeding risk and provoking factors.
High-risk PE requires urgent expert/critical-care evaluation for reperfusion therapy; intermediate-high risk requires close monitored care for deterioration.
Selected low-risk patients can be managed outpatient only when clinical and social safety criteria are met.
medicationSafety: Thrombolysis carries major bleeding risk and is not routine for stable low-risk PE.
DOACs are unsuitable in some pregnancy, severe renal, drug-interaction or other special contexts; select therapy deliberately.
counselling: Teach anticoagulant adherence, bleeding precautions and recurrence symptoms; explain whether the event was provoked/unprovoked and how that affects duration review.
followUp: Reassess anticoagulation duration, bleeding, recurrence and persistent dyspnea; evaluate chronic thromboembolic disease when symptoms persist.
examTrap: Using a positive D-dimer as proof of PE—or choosing thrombolysis for a stable patient because the CT shows a large clot burden.
oneLinePearl: Probability finds PE; hemodynamics and right-heart risk determine how aggressively it is treated.
sourceBasis: Thrombosis Canada current Pulmonary Embolism Treatment clinical guide
Thrombosis Canada current High- and Intermediate-Risk PE guide

title: Lung Cancer Screening: Screen High-Risk Asymptomatic People, Diagnose Symptoms
bottomLine: Low-dose CT screening is for asymptomatic people who meet the current provincial/territorial high-risk program criteria and are healthy enough to benefit from treatment. Hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, suspicious nodes or other cancer symptoms require diagnostic evaluation—not enrollment in a screening pathway.
recognize: Smoking history, age and additional risk-model variables determine eligibility in organized Canadian programs; exact criteria vary by province and evolve over time.
Screening can reduce lung-cancer mortality in appropriately selected high-risk populations but also causes false positives, incidental findings and downstream procedures.
differentiate: Screening and diagnostic CT are not interchangeable: screening assumes no cancer symptoms.
An incidental pulmonary nodule discovered outside a screening program follows a separate nodule-risk pathway.
assessment: Assess current/prior smoking exposure, age, prior cancer/COPD, family history, functional status/life expectancy, willingness/fitness for curative treatment and symptoms suggesting current cancer.
Use non-stigmatizing smoking history and offer cessation support regardless of screening eligibility.
workup: Refer potentially eligible asymptomatic patients through the current organized provincial/territorial lung-screening program rather than applying an outdated national age/pack-year rule universally.
Symptomatic patients need diagnostic imaging/workup based on presentation.
management: Use program-driven low-dose CT intervals and nodule management when eligible; ensure every abnormal screen has closed-loop follow-up.
Do not screen low-risk people simply because they request a CT after discussing harms/benefits.
Provide evidence-based smoking cessation support as part of prevention.
medicationSafety: Screening itself is nonpharmacologic, but downstream contrast/biopsy/procedures should be ordered only when risk warrants them and patient-specific renal/bleeding risks are considered.
counselling: Explain that screening looks for cancer before symptoms and that eligibility is based on expected benefit, not blame for smoking history.
Discuss false positives and the need to complete follow-up if an abnormality is found.
followUp: Track referral, eligibility assessment, LDCT results and downstream surveillance to definitive resolution.
Reassess eligibility later when a program recommends it if current risk is below threshold.
examTrap: Sending a patient with unexplained hemoptysis into a screening program instead of a diagnostic lung-cancer workup—or applying one old Canada-wide age/pack-year rule despite current provincial programs.
sourceBasis: Ontario Lung Screening Program current organized screening pathway
Public Health Agency of Canada preventive-guideline transition context
